"The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security," Trump wrote in a statement. queue.opening: While many Americans are still wondering what the results of the midterm elections will mean for their day-to-day lives, the Supreme Court is preparing to hear oral arguments for two cases that could impact millions of law-abiding gun owners around the country immediately. If you own a gun, or care about the Second Amendment, these cases are about you. On Dec. 2, the Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in Viramontes v. Cook County and Grant v. Higgins. Both cases before the Court challenge laws that ban so-called "assault weapons," a political label for semiautomatic rifles. It’s a scare-term designed to obscure reality and make ordinary rifles sound fringe and scary. Both laws before the Court ban the AR-15 by name and outlaw similar semiautomatic rifles based on features like an adjustable stock, a pistol grip, or a flash suppressor. These laws are unconstitutional and unfairly target law-abiding Americans. The Second Amendment Foundation has been in this fight since 2019, having filed 9 cases challenging these exact types of laws across the nation. As a plaintiff in both cases before the Supreme Court, SAF has stuck with these cases while lower courts rubber-stamped both bans. And despite years of slow and expensive litigation, the nation’s highest court will finally hear argument. queue.opening: An archaeologist may have finally solved the mystery of the unknown skeleton buried on the grounds of Westminster Abbey, one of London's most popular tourist sites — and the answer points to a 1,000-year-old recycling job. The research centers on an unidentified skeleton that was found at Westminster Abbey in 1869, according to news agency SWNS. The skeleton was found inside a Roman limestone sarcophagus bearing an inscription for Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy 4th-century Briton — but the remains inside don't belong to him. STARTLING MYSTERY REVEALED IN CENTURIES-OLD ROYAL TOMBS AT POWERFUL QUEEN'S MONASTERY When the skeleton was excavated at Westminster Abbey in 1869, archaeologists noticed that a distinctive early medieval Latin cross was sculpted on the lid. The symbol puzzled experts for over 150 years because it didn't match the Roman-era casket. The recent study, published in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association, was led by Warwick Rodwell, a consultant archaeologist at Westminster Abbey, SWNS said. Rodwell's work followed a 2025 excavation of the Abbey's vestry, which was required ahead of construction on the new King Charles III Sacristy set to open in 2027. queue.title: The End of Math?
queue.dek: AI just solved the most famous problem in modern math. Where does that leave mathematicians like me?
queue.opening: I remember the day my dad taught me that math could be beautiful. We were sitting in my parents’ office in our home in Norway. I was 13. My dad sat at one of the two desks, opposite a wall of floor-to-ceiling bookshelves full of old Russian math and literature books, their spines worn and tired from being opened and pored over for hours at a time. Next to him was a large whiteboard, which was always covered in Greek letters and strange curves depicting various mathematical equations. Those in red ink were my dad’s; those in blue, my mom’s. My parents were immigrants who came to the city of Trondheim from the former Soviet Union to research and teach math at one of Norway’s most prestigious science and technical universities. Math was our family’s love language. It was how my parents met. It was also the subject of many a dinnertime conversation in my home growing up. My parents would start with a question like: “What if alpha goes to zero faster than beta?” My sister and I would roll our eyes at times, but we also found it charming, especially when we would watch our dad rattle off a theorem about Fourier analysis as if he were reciting an old Russian poem. queue.dek: Ross Stores reported a 12% jump in third-quarter sales as shoppers sought bargains, but rising fuel expenses and a cautious holiday forecast pressured shares.
queue.opening: More shoppers are heading to Ross Stores in search of bargains, pushing the discount retailer’s third-quarter sales up 12% — yet shares still slipped Friday as higher fuel costs and a slower holiday sales forecast tempered investor enthusiasm. The off-price retailer, which operates Ross Dress for Less and dd's DISCOUNTS , brought in $6.26 billion in sales for the quarter ended Oct. 31, up from $5.6 billion a year earlier, according to its Nov. 19 earnings release. Sales at stores open at least a year jumped 8%, fueled largely by more shoppers walking through the doors. Net income climbed to $606 million, or $1.91 per share, beating the company’s own profit targets. But even with the strong quarter, Ross Stores shares still closed down 2.92% on Friday at $213.46. Investors appeared cautious after the company maintained its forecast for 4% to 5% same-store sales growth during the holiday quarter — a step down from its third-quarter pace and last year’s 9% holiday surge. queue.title: Indonesia candy factory fire leaves multiple dead, dozens missing
queue.dek: A massive fire tore through PT Fonusa Agung Mulia's candy factory in Indonesia's Banten, killing at least three with up to 50 workers missing.
queue.opening: A massive fire tore through a three-story candy factory in Indonesia's Banten province, killing at least three workers and likely more, and leaving dozens of others unaccounted for as emergency crews fought persistent hotspots into Sunday. Indonesian police removed 24 body bags amid battling the smoldering fire and pausing a search for missing workers overnight, which will resume Monday morning. There were reportedly as many as 300 present for their Saturday shift, but the factory said 24 of the 65 workers involved had returned home, four were receiving medical treatment, 29 remained missing and the whereabouts of another eight had yet to be confirmed. Body bags might contain remains from several people because the intensity of the fire had rendered the recovered victims unidentifiable, police said. The fire broke out at 5 p.m. local time Saturday at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia facility in the Cikande area of the Serang district, which borders the capital, Jakarta. Authorities are collecting DNA samples from relatives and personal belongings of the missing workers. The identification process could take two to three weeks, Hidayati added. queue.title: Newsom's bid to empty California's death row collides with voters' repeated rejection of abolition
queue.dek: A lawsuit challenges Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom's effort to commute all 548 death sentences, citing failures to notify district attorneys.
queue.opening: A lawsuit challenging Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute 548 death sentences is raising questions about the governor's clemency powers, with a legal expert arguing Newsom is using his gubernatorial authority to circumvent the will of voters who have repeatedly rejected efforts to abolish capital punishment. Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he intends to commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates on the Golden State's death row to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole, a move that will take effect only after the necessary legal steps are completed. The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation (CJLF) on Sunday filed a lawsuit at the California Supreme Court seeking to block Newsom's proposed sweeping commutation, citing the governor's "failure to provide legally required notice to district attorneys and his disregard for the rights of victims and their families to be notified and heard," according to a news release. Newsom may be using clemency to impose his own views on capital punishment despite voters repeatedly rejecting abolition, Zack Smith, a senior legal fellow for Courts and the Constitution at the Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital on Tuesday. queue.dek: Investors behind a False Claims Act qui tam lawsuit over Crescent Dunes' $275 million federal grant say the Trump DOJ is defending a Biden-era dismissal.
queue.opening: This article is Part 2 of a Fox News Digital exclusive series investigating the Crescent Dunes solar power plant in Nevada. You can read Part 1 here . The Trump administration has made fighting fraud and rooting out government waste a top priority, even offering cash rewards to Americans who expose wrongdoing. Yet investors in a failed Obama-era solar plant are questioning why President Donald Trump's own Justice Department is fighting to squash their fraud lawsuit over a $275 million federal grant — a case they say could recover up to $1 billion for taxpayers. The investors allege that Spanish construction giant ACS and companies to tied its former subsidiary Cobra, misled federal officials into approving the grant by claiming the troubled solar plant was ready for use, even though it had suffered major construction problems and was shut down for months following a molten-salt-tank failure. The lawsuit centers on the beleaguered Crescent Dunes solar plant, a billion-dollar, government-backed project that began operating in Nevada in 2015 but was later plagued by engineering failures, repeated shutdowns and two bankruptcies before being sold for just $7 million in July. queue.title: NYC college put on notice after Jewish campus group shunned by student government: 'Rude awakening'
queue.dek: Shabbos Kestenbaum decries anti-Jewish discrimination after a City University of New York school canceled a Cultural Arts Night, citing Title VI.
queue.opening: A Jewish American activist in New York City decried what he calls "anti-Jewish discrimination" after the student government at a school that is part of the City University of New York (CUNY) system, canceled an event that was supposed to include the school's Hillel group when it received backlash from other student organizations. Hunter College's undergraduate student government (USG) canceled a "Cultural Arts Night" involving several student groups, including Hunter Hillel, the Chinese Student & Scholar Association, the Taiwanese Student Association and the Center for Puerto Rican Studies, according to the New York Post . The radical far-left group Students for Justice in Palestine reportedly took part in planning the event. In a statement to The Post, the school itself admitted that some of those groups withdrew from the event because Hunter Hillel was planning to participate. queue.title: What We Don’t Know About the Iran War
Jeffries calling Jerusalem NYC's ‘sixth borough’ resurfaces as progressives swing against Israel
queue.dek: Hakeem Jeffries once called Jerusalem the "6th Borough" in a resurfaced AIPAC clip, raising questions as he heads toward a January House speaker vote.
queue.opening: Hakeem Jeffries once called his deep ties to Jerusalem an extension of his representation of New York City as he touted his support for Israel and the Jewish community. But those comments from 2020, recently resurfaced and going viral, may come back to bite the Democratic House leader as the progressive wing of the party — and even some establishment members — continue to further break with the U.S. maintaining support for the Jewish state. "Someone said to me, ‘Hakeem, you’re going to Israel a 5th time?’" Jeffries recalled in an interview with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) more than six years ago. "I said, ‘listen, I’m from New York City' — and back home in New York City, we consider Jerusalem to be the 6th Borough. And so, I’m just trying to catch up with my constituents." The comments resurfaced just after he won his party's nomination to be speaker of the House in the next Congress. JEFFRIES SURVIVES DEM VOTE TO SECURE SPEAKER POSITION AS PROGRESSIVE RESISTANCE CLOUDS HIS CHANCES The remarks from 2020 contrast starkly with a growing faction of the Democratic Party that has condemned AIPAC and the political favor Israel has historically enjoyed among lawmakers. The clip also raises questions over how far Jeffries will go to placate calls for a more critical review of U.S.-Israel relations in light of his previous support for the Jewish state.
